prompt: Statements about binary max-heaps — which two are correct?
options: The largest element sits at the root.
A binary max-heap is always a binary search tree.
Deleting the maximum, then moving the last node of the heap to the root, then running heapify, again yields a valid binary max-heap.
In a binary max-heap the largest elements are located in the leaves.
explanation: The heap property (parent ≥ children) forces the maximum to the root ✓, and move-last-to-root + sift-down is exactly the standard extract-max ✓. A heap has no left/right ordering, so it is not a BST ✗, and the *smallest* elements end up in the leaves ✗.

prompt: Array representation of a binary heap (0-indexed) — which two statements are correct?
options: The children of index i are at 2i+1 and 2i+2.
The parent of index i is at ⌊(i−1)/2⌋.
The heap needs an explicit pointer per node, since the tree structure cannot be derived from indices.
The array representation only works if the number of elements is a power of two.
explanation: The index arithmetic ✓✓ is exactly what makes the representation implicit — no pointers are stored at all ✗. Completeness of the tree (every level full except possibly the last, filled left to right) is what makes the arithmetic valid, and that holds for any n ✗.

prompt: During sift-down (heapify) at node i in a max-heap, node i is smaller than both of its children. What must happen?
options: Swap i with the *larger* of its two children, then continue sifting down from that position.
Swap i with the smaller of its two children.
Swap i with both children simultaneously.
Nothing — the heap property still holds.
explanation: Swapping with the smaller child would leave the larger child above its new parent, so the violation would persist on that side. Only promoting the larger child restores parent ≥ both children locally, after which the recursion fixes the subtree it was swapped into.

prompt: BuildHeap — which two statements are correct?
options: Only about the first half of the indices needs a heapify call, because the remaining ones are leaves with no children to violate the property against.
It must proceed bottom-up, because heapify(A, i) is only correct if both children of i are already valid heaps.
The obvious bound n/2 · O(log n) is tight, so BuildHeap is Θ(n log n).
Top-down and bottom-up both yield a valid heap; only the constant factor differs.
explanation: Skipping the leaf half ✓ and the bottom-up requirement ✓ are the two structural facts. A tighter analysis gives Θ(n), because most calls happen near the leaves where a sift-down travels only 1–2 levels ✗. And top-down is not merely slower — it is *wrong*: once the root has been processed it is never revisited, so deep large values can never bubble up ✗.

prompt: Insert into a binary max-heap — which two statements are correct?
options: The new key is appended at the last free slot, because that is the only position preserving completeness, then sifted up.
Sift-up terminates as soon as the parent is ≥ the key, after at most ⌈log n⌉ comparisons.
Appending and then re-running the full BuildHeap is incorrect and produces an invalid heap.
The new key is inserted at the root and sifted down.
explanation: Append-then-sift-up ✓ costs at most one root-to-leaf path ✓. Append + full BuildHeap is *correct but wasteful* — it re-checks ⌈(n−1)/2⌉ nodes to fix what one path already handles ✗. Inserting at the root would overwrite the maximum ✗.

prompt: Is Heap Sort stable and/or in place?
options: In place, but not stable
Stable, but not in place
Both stable and in place
Neither stable nor in place
explanation: Heap Sort works entirely within the original array with O(1) extra space ⟹ in place. But the long-range swaps of sift-down and the swap-root-with-last step can reorder equal keys, so it is not stable.

prompt: Structural properties of heaps — which two statements are correct?
options: The heap property compares a node only to its direct children, so the second-largest element may sit anywhere on the second level.
A max-heap of n elements has height Θ(log n), because it is a complete binary tree.
An ascendingly sorted array always satisfies the max-heap property.
In a max-heap the third-largest element is guaranteed to lie at depth 2.
explanation: The property is purely local ✓, and completeness forces height Θ(log n) ✓. An ascending array is a valid *min*-heap, not a max-heap ✗, and no position guarantee beyond "not above a larger ancestor" exists for the third-largest element ✗.

prompt: Heaps as priority queues — which two statements are correct?
options: peek-max is O(1), while insert and extract-max are O(log n).
Neither insert nor extract-max ever performs a rotation — only swaps along a single path.
Building a heap from an unsorted array costs Θ(n log n).
A priority queue backed by a sorted array gives O(1) insert.
explanation: The priority-queue cost profile ✓ and the absence of rotations ✓ are both standard exam points (the latter is exactly why heaps appear in the "needs no rotation function" question). BuildHeap is Θ(n) ✗, and a sorted array needs Θ(n) per insert to keep order ✗.
